mt_river_wall.blurb: A small riverside wall in Stillwater Canyon, part of the Point of Rocks climbing near Kalispell. It holds eleven routes, mostly trad lines with three bolted sport leads, on quartzite. Grades run from an easy 5.7 up to 5.12, with the bulk of the climbing in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it suits climbers at a solid intermediate level or above. The face looks north and sits just above the water, which keeps it comfortable on days when most other crags in the northwest corner of the state are too hot. Expect a short drop into the canyon to reach it.

mt_bud_wall_the.blurb: A blue-streaked wall high in Wolverine Bowl, a sub-alpine climbing basin in the Bridger Range outside Bozeman, at roughly 7,900 feet. Eleven mostly bolted lines run from about 5.7 to 5.11, with most clustering around 5.10, which makes it a handy spot for warm-ups and moderates in a bowl better known for harder, steeper climbing. The base is a small ledge with a few trees, reached by working up past the two Replica cliffs across scree. Plan on a long hike in from the lower trailhead, and bring water and a helmet at this elevation.

mt_main_area_2.blurb: The first formation you meet on the walk up to The Palace, above Palisade Campground near Red Lodge. It is a large palisade-style wall with routes facing every direction, so there is usually shade or sun to chase. Eleven bolted sport lines on limestone cover a wide spread, from an easy 5.6 through several 5.9 and 5.10 leads to a handful of 5.12 and 5.13 test pieces. The area is still being developed and the rock is fair rather than polished, so bring a helmet and a brush. Expect a steep hike of ten to thirty minutes from the car.
mt_main_area_2.parking_note: Leave the car at the Palisade Campground parking area outside Red Lodge; the trail to the formation starts there.

mt_voyage_wall.blurb: A tall limestone fin at the heart of Maiden Rocks, a secluded sport-climbing destination between Butte and Dillon, and visible from the drive in. All eleven routes are bolted, steep and long, and the grades skew hard: most sit in the 5.13 and 5.14 range, with one 5.12 and a single easy outing. The climbing blends power with technique and rewards good beta. Reach it by walking uphill from the neighbouring Momentum Wall; an open slot on the right gives access to the easier lines. This is a wall for strong sport climbers.

mt_zig_zag_crag.blurb: A small crag in the Gash Creek drainage outside Victor, reached by a winding forest road. It has eleven routes, a roughly even mix of trad cracks and bolted sport lines, with some top-rope options. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, and most of the climbing falls around 5.11, so it is best for confident leaders; there is a good 5.9 for those warming up. The wall is shaded through the morning and picks up sun in the early afternoon. Bring about fourteen quickdraws and a single rack to three inches.

mt_alberton_rest_stop.blurb: A roadside crag about 36 miles west of Missoula, next to the interstate rest area near Alberton. Eleven routes, mostly bolted with a couple of trad lines, are spread over a main wall and slabby sections off to the sides. Grades range from 5.6 to 5.12, with gentle slab climbing on the side trails and a steep, demanding main wall that is usually shaded and chilly in autumn. The quartzite is good quality. It is a quick stop for a few pitches rather than a full-day destination, with the walk from the car only a short way downhill.
mt_alberton_rest_stop.parking_note: Park in the rest-stop lot just off the highway; the main wall is a short walk down the slope below it.

mt_1_upper_moriah_s_ledge.blurb: The top tier of Moriah's Ledges in the Stone Hill climbing zone near Kalispell, one level beneath Room with a View. Ten routes split on either side of a descent chimney: six trad, three sport and one top-rope line, from about 5.6 to 5.11. Four climbs fall in the 5.10 range, with a few easier cracks at the low end, so it works for a mixed party. Anchors allow an easy top-rope setup. The ledges stay shaded until around one in the afternoon and are breezy, pleasant on hot days. The approach from the road takes under five minutes.

mt_behind_the_curtain.blurb: A hidden pocket of gneiss boulders in the Cascade Creek bouldering zone of Gallatin Canyon, near Big Sky, about halfway up the Lava Lake trail at around 6,400 feet. Three blocs tucked in the trees, a few yards from the path, hold ten problems that stretch from an easy V1 to a pair of V9s, with a cluster around V4 and some projects left. Tree cover keeps the spot shaded all day, so it is cooler than the open talus nearby on hot afternoons, though surfaces can be mossy. A large rock marks the turn-off from the trail.

_conflicts.mt_bud_wall_the: Stored rock is quartzite, but the Wolverine Bowl page describes blue Madison limestone: https://www.mountainproject.com/area/109341880/wolverine-bowl
